Hi
I did exactly the same, on more or less the same species in French Guiana. =
The Detection function is, in most of the cases, not different between hunt=
ed in non hunted sites. I think that the density of the forest is the stron=
ger constraint so that the fleeing distances does not vary so much (animals=
escape more rapidly in hunted places, but not from so much longer distance=
s , I think) So just test before if the detection fonctions are not the sam=
e in your case, so that you can pool the data across sites to get the ESW, =
and then get a site by site dentity. I agree that it will never be enough f=
or some very rare species, but it will be usefull for all the common ones.
Carlos Peres also tested that between-sites variance in PD are not greater =
than the within sites (ANOVA), before pooling the perp distances .
Sincerely.

bjet=A0: generating robust estimates for rare species (hunted vs. non-hunte=
d tropical forest)

Hello all,

I have a follow-up question to one I posed earlier. I completed a tra=
nsect study of primates and large frugivorous birds across three tropical f=
orest sites in Peru. The sites are under varying degrees of hunting pressu=
re, with one intact site, one moderate site, and one highly impacted site. =
My survey effort at each site was just over 100km, and the Distance analys=
is was done on a site-by-site basis, with no pooling or stratification. Gi=
ven that some of my target species occur at very low densities as a result =
of hunting pressures, the data and resulting Distance analysis is not very =
robust. I have a few questions in response to this:

1. How does one generate a robust density estimate for a species which is =
so rarely encountered? My understanding is that pooling the data for a giv=
en species across all three sites would be inappropriate in this case, as t=
he detectability of that species is not the same across sites (the animals =
at a hunted site will respond by avoiding surveyors and fleeing more quickl=
y and quietly, thus they will be less detectable than at an intact site, wh=
ich will skew the estimates).

2. It seems that generating a good density estimate of a rarely encountere=
d species would require an astronomical amount of survey effort. Is there =
a consensus guideline for the minimum recommended effort? I have read that=
40 observations is a good general minimum, but that is an unreasonable goa=
l for a rare species...

3. If after 10 weeks of intensive field study, I am not able to generate e=
nough data for a robust density estimate of a rarely encountered species, h=
ow useful is Distance as a conservation tool for assessing populations of r=
are species?

I have read through the Distance Sampling book and several additional =
publications guiding the sampling of tropical forest primates, but I am not=
able to find specific answers to these questions. I would appreciate any =
feedback or suggestions on how to proceed with my analysis. If you have qu=
estions in response to my post, I would be happy to elaborate. If this is a=
recurring question among the Distance community, I would gladly compile th=
e responses to this post to share. Thanks very much for your time!! Since=
rely,


Cooper Rosin
